solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sailor that could make a meal with beans

indicators.note: to make something from raw ingredients is to rework them, so these letters get rearranged into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship's cook boasts of the dish he could rustle up from a tin of beans.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes 'a meal' and 'beans' together, ten letters that become ABLE SEAMAN; the surface reads like a recipe, which the kitchen words disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: An able seaman is a rank of trained naval rating, so the phrase names a kind of sailor.

clue.text: Anxiously awaiting a hiding to nothing ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so each word gives up only its final letter

blocks.note: the closing letters of the four words in turn

explanation.surface: Someone waits nervously for a contest they are certain to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hiding to nothing' is an idiom for a task you cannot win, so it reads as one phrase; here it is just four words whose last letters spell AGOG.
explanation.definitionFit: Agog describes eager, excited expectation, the state of someone keenly waiting for news to arrive.

clue.text: Alcoholic drinks from club I found during Pride?

indicators.note: something found during an event sits within its span, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a bat is a club used in games like cricket
taken as written
a pride is a group of lions, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone finds a club serving cocktails during a Pride celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: Pride with a capital looks like the LGBT festival, but it is the collective noun for lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Libations are, loosely and humorously, alcoholic beverages; strictly the word means drink poured out as an offering.

clue.text: Located high-grade tissue boxes on the counter

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the wanted run of letters is held inside the words
counter means contrary or opposite, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: letters straddling the end of grade and the start of tissue

explanation.surface: Quality tissue boxes are found sitting on a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' and 'counter' look like shop nouns; one signals the letters are tucked inside 'grade tissue', the other that they read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sited is to be placed or positioned somewhere, the same meaning as located.

clue.text: Maintenance of whichever luxury car breaks

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: short for limousine
any one at all

explanation.surface: Whatever expensive car you own, it needs servicing when it breaks down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maintenance' suggests car servicing, but it is the legal sense of money paid to a former spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Alimony is court-ordered financial support paid to an ex-spouse, which British law calls maintenance.

clue.text: Reach a church one day before

blocks.note: taken as written
CH is the standard abbreviation for church
the Roman numeral for one
an eve is the day before an event, as in Christmas Eve

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives at a church on the day before a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Every piece is a crossword staple: CH for church, I for one, EVE for the day before.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve a goal is to attain or arrive at it, matching the figurative sense of reach.

clue.text: Great book in my opinion

blocks.note: first meaning: a large, heavy volume
second meaning: read as two words, the phrase 'as far as I am concerned'

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a reviewer's verdict; the second meaning only works if you split the answer into two words, TO ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A tome is a large, weighty volume, and 'to me' is the idiom expressing personal view.

clue.text: Regularly got naked to have following on X

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters come off and the core is kept

blocks.note: the central letter once the outer two are stripped
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone keeps stripping off to win followers on the social network X.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the former Twitter, a place to gain a following; it is simply the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Often and regularly both describe something happening many times or frequently.

clue.text: Bush Senior and Barbara evoked Ronald Reagan years initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up only its opening letter

blocks.note: an elder is someone older or senior
the leading letters of these five words

explanation.surface: George Bush Senior and his wife Barbara brought back memories of the Reagan era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush Senior' looks like one name, George H. W. Bush, but 'Bush' is the definition and 'Senior' the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The elderberry is a shrub of the genus Sambucus bearing dark fruit, so it is a bush.

clue.text: Circuit court regularly fell for it

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
to bite is to take the bait, so 'bit' means was taken in

explanation.surface: A circuit court judge was regularly taken in by a defendant's story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circuit court' is a real legal term, which hides that 'Circuit' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbit is the curved path one body travels around another, a complete circuit or revolution.

clue.text: Came into discontented institution he tried to change

indicators.note: without contents means emptied, so only the outside letters remain
a change alters the arrangement, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: first and last letters with the middle gone
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone joined an unhappy organisation that he had tried to reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' reads as unhappy staff; cryptically it empties the word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into money or property is the idiom for receiving it through a will, as an heir.

clue.text: Comic possibly seen removing top after run

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter, so that letter is taken away
coming after means placed later in the line, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
able to be seen

explanation.surface: A comedian might be spotted taking his shirt off after a jog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' looks like a person, the comedian, but it is an adjective here, meaning laughable.
explanation.definitionFit: Risible means provoking laughter or ridicule, which is one sense of the adjective comic.

clue.text: Staff splash first young swimmer

indicators.note: first sets the order, saying which part leads the line

blocks.note: a splash, as of milk, is a small amount, as is a tad
a staff is a long stick or rod

explanation.surface: Pool staff are told to splash the youngest swimmer first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees but is a stick; 'young swimmer' sounds like a child at a pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the larval stage of a frog or toad, living and swimming in water.

clue.text: Sierra with funny Nora Batty navigation system!

indicators.note: funny means peculiar or odd, hinting that letters are jumbled
batty means crazy, so the preceding letters go wild and change order

blocks.note: Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nora Batty, a comic character, is paired with a Ford Sierra and a satnav.
explanation.walkthrough: Nora Batty is the stocking-wearing character from the British sitcom Last of the Summer Wine; her surname doubles as the anagram signal, and Sierra is also a Ford car model.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonar uses sound pulses to detect objects underwater, helping ships and submarines navigate and find things.

clue.text: Unfortunately royal bigot is unavoidable

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A prejudiced member of the royal family is, sadly, something we cannot escape.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten letters of 'royal bigot' rearrange exactly, and 'is' joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obligatory is compulsory or required, and so cannot be avoided by anyone.

clue.text: Times describing bad drive as hair-raising experience?

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: by means multiplied by, as in three by four
low as in base or mean
DR is the address abbreviation for Drive

explanation.surface: A newspaper reports that a terrifying car journey was a hair-raising ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign; 'hair-raising' is taken literally, with a question mark flagging the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow-dry lifts and styles hair with a hand-held dryer, so it literally raises the hair.

clue.text: Resentment of failure having no say after retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a dud is something that fails to work
taken as written
e.g. means for example, as does say

explanation.surface: A retired person resents being ignored once they have stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No say after retirement' sounds like a pensioner's grievance; the turnaround applies to 'no say' alone, and 'say' is the familiar EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon means a feeling of offence or deep indignation, usually in the phrase 'in high dudgeon'.

clue.text: Focus of ceremony before couple hug

indicators.note: a focus is a central point, so only the middle of the word is kept
before sets the order, placing one part ahead of the next

blocks.note: the central pair of letters in this eight-letter word
a brace is a pair, as of pheasants

explanation.surface: The highlight of a wedding comes as the newly married couple hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' suggests the wedding pair; here it is BRACE, a word for two of anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace someone is to hold them closely in your arms, which is a hug.

clue.text: Moving - as stopgap accepting offer after banks withdraw

indicators.note: a word's banks are its edges, and when they withdraw only the inside is left
to accept is to take in, so one piece receives another inside it

blocks.note: an acting head serves temporarily until a permanent one is found
the inner letters with first and last gone

explanation.surface: A temporary arrangement takes up an offer as the banks pull out of a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks financial but means the edges of a word; 'Moving' is the emotional sense, not relocation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something affecting stirs emotion, touching the feelings in the same way as a moving story.

clue.text: Hot drink picked up for one of us

indicators.note: to pick something up is to hear it, as a radio picks up a signal

blocks.note: hot means fashionable or in, and cider is an apple drink

explanation.surface: Someone collects a hot drink for one of the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot drink' suggests tea or coffee; it is two pieces, IN for fashionable and CIDER, said together.
explanation.definitionFit: An insider belongs to a group or organisation, someone within the circle rather than outside it.

clue.text: Recycled clothes female turned down

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece dresses another

blocks.note: recycled things are used again
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman rejected second-hand clothing that was offered to her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun for garments; it is the verb, to dress or cover.
explanation.definitionFit: To be refused is to be rejected or declined, the same as being turned down.

clue.text: Enjoys attacks

blocks.note: first meaning: likes or favours, as in a taste for something
second meaning: lunges at, as a dog might

explanation.walkthrough: Two words with nothing else; the phrasal verb works both for liking something and for assaulting someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to favour or prefer something and to launch an assault on someone.

clue.text: Piano make with 50 per cent off for family member

indicators.note: half off means half the word is lost, keeping only the front portion

blocks.note: a grand is a large concert piano
taken as written before cutting

explanation.surface: A piano brand is offered at half price as a present for a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' looks like a brand name in the surface; it is simply the word, cut in half.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandma is a grandmother, a relative two generations up, so she is a family member.

clue.text: Liberal politician framed by porter?

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
porter is a dark beer, an example of ale, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat MP has been set up by a hotel porter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal politician' reads as one party member, and 'porter' as a doorman; the definition is the adjective liberal, generous.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample and liberal both describe a generous quantity, more than enough of something.

clue.text: One doesn't believe name a clothes shop rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters return the other way

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
taken as written
Gap is an American chain of clothing stores

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to trust a clothing retailer that turned down their name.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run of name, a and the shop is turned round together, not just the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagan does not hold the beliefs of the main world religions, so is called an unbeliever.

clue.text: Mad tirade one's written in Liverpool, say

indicators.note: writing in a space puts text inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a rant is an angry tirade
one is I, the Roman numeral, and 's stands for is
Liverpool is an example of a football club, FC

explanation.surface: An angry rant has been penned in Liverpool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liverpool, say' looks like the city; it is the football team, an example of an FC.
explanation.definitionFit: Frantic describes wild, desperate agitation, close to being mad with worry or emotion.

clue.text: Everyone trusts this every now and then

indicators.note: now and then means at intervals, so letters are kept at regular spacing

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A statement about the universal faith people place in something.
explanation.walkthrough: TUTTI is a musical direction from Italian telling the whole ensemble to play together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti is Italian for all, used in scores to mean every performer plays at once.

clue.text: Possibly does article in Bild without English

indicators.note: without can mean outside, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: der is a German definite article, and Bild is a German newspaper
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone writes a piece for the German tabloid Bild without using English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like a verb, and 'without' like 'lacking'; both are in their other senses, female deer and outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Does are female deer, so deer could possibly be does; the 'possibly' flags the definition by example.

clue.text: Journalist on publication is certainly not 24 Across

indicators.note: on means placed after, in the order an across answer reads

blocks.note: an organ is a periodical speaking for a group
taken as written
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A reporter writing for a paper insists he is calm, not frantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 Across is FRANTIC, so the definition asks for its opposite; ORGAN for a party newspaper is a common crossword sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone organised is orderly and in control, the opposite of being wild, panicked and frantic.

clue.text: Banal tips from trainer and Aintree odds must be cut

indicators.note: tips are the ends, so only the outer letters are kept
cutting the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

blocks.note: first and last letters
the second, fourth and sixth letters remain

explanation.surface: A racehorse trainer's tips for Aintree are dull and the betting odds must be shortened.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree is the Liverpool racecourse that hosts the Grand National; 'tips' and 'odds' are racing words doing letter work here.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite and banal both describe remarks that are overused, stale and lacking any originality.

clue.text: Hairy Tibetan welcoming North American

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: the yak is a shaggy ox of Tibet
N is the abbreviation for North

explanation.surface: A shaggy-haired Tibetan greets a visitor from North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North American' looks like one phrase; North belongs to the wordplay and American alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is an informal, often British, nickname for a person from the United States.

clue.text: Jack sad about delay for writer

indicators.note: about can mean around or astir, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack
taken as written
to linger is to tarry or delay

explanation.surface: A man called Jack is unhappy about a hold-up in hearing from a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it scrambles the three letters that follow J.
explanation.definitionFit: J. D. Salinger was the American novelist who wrote The Catcher in the Rye, so he is a writer.
